quote: Howson is a leading advocate for an alternative view of science based not on simplistic true/false logic, but on the far more subtle concept of degrees of belief. At its heart is a fundamental connection between the subjective concept of belief and the cold, hard mathematics of probability.
content: The essay is right that it is less of an iconoclast than it seems, and the point cuts deeper than it allows. Bayesian philosophy of science had been a mainstream position for two decades by 2008 (Howson and Urbach, 1989; Earman, 1992; the Bayesian confirmation theory of Jeffrey, Salmon and Rosenkrantz before them), and Howson himself is on record against the commitment that makes this book’s Bayesianism distinctive: he argued that there is no objective sense in which simpler theories are a priori more probable, and that the prior is genuinely the agent’s (Howson, “On the Consistency of Jeffreys’s Simplicity Postulate, and Its Role in Bayesian Inference,” Philosophical Quarterly, 1988). So the “mainstream let’s-reformulate-Science-as-Bayesianism” that the essay claims kinship with does not endorse the Solomonoff–Occam apparatus on which the quantum sequence’s verdicts depend, and would regard the claim that many-worlds is “strictly simpler” as a substantive and contestable prior rather than a theorem. The three points of departure the essay lists (not being in academia, needing more than probability theory, believing one can do better) are not the one that matters, which is that the essay’s Bayesianism carries an objectivist theory of simplicity that most Bayesian philosophers of science reject.

quote: First time you ever see an apple fall down, you observe the position goes as the square of time, invent calculus, generalize Newton’s Laws… and see that Newton’s Laws involve action at a distance, look for alternative explanations with increased locality, invent relativistic covariance around a hypothetical speed limit, and consider that General Relativity might be worth testing.
content: The apple does not contain the information. A falling apple, however precisely observed, shows constant acceleration; it is equally consistent with a uniform downward field and with an inverse-square law, and the datum that distinguishes them is the Moon, whose centripetal acceleration Newton compared with the apple’s to get the 1/r2 (the “Moon test” in the Principia, Book III). No amount of intelligence extracts from one trajectory a law about how the field varies with distance, because the trajectory samples one distance. The further steps need Maxwell’s equations and a measured c for relativity, and the equivalence of inertial and gravitational mass, an empirical fact from Eötvös’s torsion balance, for the road to general relativity. What a superintelligence could do from an apple is generate hypotheses, including these; what it could not do is confirm them, and the essay conflates the two throughout this sequence. The automated-science experiments that have been run make the point: a system that rediscovered conservation laws from motion data needed many trajectories over varied conditions to do it (Schmidt & Lipson (2009)). Information, not cleverness, was the binding constraint, as the essay’s own Solomonoff bound says it must be.
